SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability ResearchThanks: Preprint. This work has not yet been peer reviewed.

Amine Lbath14, Manan Suri3, Aurelien Delaitre1, Vadim Okun1, Massih-Reza Amini4 and Dinesh Manocha3 Affiliation: 1National Institute of Standards and Technology Affiliation: 4Université Grenoble Alpes, CNRS Affiliation: 3University of Maryland, College Park Affiliation: 
Abstract

LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities in real-world software without human intervention before the restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records, advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived a decade or more in widely used code were reported several times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages of a vulnerability’s life, from report to fix and from disclosure to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the best-supported ones.

Index Terms: 
vulnerability research, LLM-based agents, autonomy levels, vulnerability lifecycle, measurement, systematization of knowledge

I Introduction

Software vulnerability research covers discovering vulnerabilities, proving that they are real and fixing them. Automated tools such as fuzzers and static analyzers can surface large numbers of candidate bugs, yet because many of these candidates are false positives, triage, proof and repair have remained the work of human experts. Recent reports suggest that LLM-based systems are increasingly capable of carrying out these steps autonomously on real software. Google’s Big Sleep agent reported zero-day vulnerabilities in real-world code as early as 2024 [1]. By 2025, a growing number of systems, among them those of DARPA’s AI Cyber Challenge (AIxCC), were finding and patching vulnerabilities in open-source projects [2, 3]. In April 2026, Anthropic reported that Claude Mythos Preview had found thousands of high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities, almost always without human intervention, and restricted the model to selected partners [4, 5]. In July 2026, agents under evaluation at OpenAI exploited a previously unknown vulnerability to leave their environment and attacked several systems, including those of Hugging Face [6].

These reports have raised concern among practitioners, who describe a “Vulnpocalypse”, a surge of findings that maintainers may be unable to absorb [7, 8]. Labs warn that exploits could follow fixes within hours [9], while others expect the supply of bugs to run out once existing code has been swept [10, 11]. Assessing these expectations requires evidence on two questions, namely what these systems have been shown to do, and what has changed so far in the vulnerability lifecycle.

Neither question is easy to answer from the published evidence. Capability reports describe tasks that range from flagging suspicious code to delivering an accepted fix, and they differ in how much a human contributed. Their correctness also varies widely, from expert precision for the best systems [12] to large numbers of invalid reports received by maintainers [13]. Many reports come from the organizations that build the systems, benchmarks tend to rely on curated targets [14], and the most capable models are often reachable only through interfaces that their developers control [15]. Statements about the consequences come from the same parties and are rarely compared with public records.

In this SoK, we address both questions and treat them as complementary. For the first, we introduce, to our knowledge, the first framework that assesses the demonstrated autonomy of LLM-based systems separately for each task of vulnerability research, over time and across levels of access. Following the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) levels of driving automation [16], we define each autonomy level by the part of the task that remains with the human. A level counts only when most of the results hold up, and every claim also receives an access tier, from internal lab use to open weights, and an evidence grade. To apply the framework, we built an agentic workflow that collected more than 50,000 unique sources, including academic publications, lab and vendor reports, maintainers’ accounts and incident disclosures. Independent agents searched this indexed corpus for the most relevant evidence on real software and scored it, supporting each score with a quote checked against the source. Two authors then reviewed the 128 dated steps of the resulting map, and our conclusions draw only on steps backed by direct evidence on real software. For the second question, we collected the consequences commonly expected of these capabilities from 503 verified statements by labs, vendors, maintainers, government agencies and researchers, and compared these expectations with a decade of public records. These comprise more than 300,000 CVE records [17] with their severity, the age of the vulnerable code where it is known, the first public exploits and the listings as exploited, as well as the timelines of about 1,400 coordinated disclosures and the records of disclosure programs.

  • RQ1: What is the current capability of LLM-based systems, in terms of autonomy and correctness, to discover, validate and patch vulnerabilities in real-world software? (Section V-A)

  • RQ2: How has this capability evolved since 2024? (Section V-B)

  • RQ3: How rapidly do capabilities first demonstrated by frontier-lab systems diffuse to publicly available and open-weight models? (Section V-C)

  • RQ4: What has changed so far in public vulnerability records, and what has not? (Section VI)

  • RQ5: Which mitigations are supported by evidence, and what guidance follows for each stakeholder? (Section VII)

In addressing these questions, this paper makes four contributions.

  • •

    Assessment framework. To our knowledge, the first framework that rates the demonstrated autonomy of LLM-based systems for four tasks of vulnerability research, together with the correctness of their results, their level of access and the strength of the evidence (Section III).

  • •

    Capability map. A reproducible, dated map of demonstrated capability since 2024 (Sections IV and V, Figure 1). Agents built it from a corpus of more than 50,000 sources, and two authors reviewed each of its steps. It shows that agents were able to discover, validate and patch real vulnerabilities without human intervention by October 2025, before the restricted frontier models of 2026, that open-weight models followed within months for discovery and validation, and that remediation is the least measured task.

  • •

    Measurement of public records. A measurement of the volume, severity and age of disclosed vulnerabilities, and of the time to fix and to attack, in a decade of public records, compared with seven commonly expected consequences (Section VI). Disclosures more than doubled in 2026, with a growing share rated Critical or High and several times more old, severe bugs, whereas the time to fix and to attack has not shifted noticeably so far.

  • •

    Mitigations and research agenda. A rubric-based grading of 15 proposed mitigations, followed by guidance for each group of stakeholders and open problems (Sections VII and VIII). The best-supported mitigations are established practices of secure design, whereas those built on LLMs are the least measured.

II Background and Related Work

Software vulnerability research. Vulnerability research begins with selecting a target and discovering a flaw, which must then be validated, usually by a proof that it can be triggered. Once the flaw is reported, the maintainer triages it, develops and validates a patch, and releases it, and operators finally deploy the fix. Under coordinated vulnerability disclosure, the finder gives the maintainer a fixed period, commonly 90 days, to release a fix before the details become public [18]. This practice presumes that discovery is scarce, so that a reported vulnerability is unlikely to be found by someone else before it is fixed. By one estimate, only about 5.7% of privately held zero-day vulnerabilities are rediscovered by others each year [19]. Deployment has also consistently lagged behind the fix. In enterprises, a patch for client software can take more than six months to reach 90% of the machines [20].

Measuring the vulnerability lifecycle. A long line of empirical work has measured the lifecycle of vulnerabilities. Zero-day attacks have been found to last 312 days on average before disclosure [21], and in one study about 7% of 4,080 security fixes failed to fully remove the vulnerability [22]. How often coordinated disclosure achieves its intended order, with the fix available before the details are public and before attacks begin, has also been modeled and measured [23]. Whether finding vulnerabilities eventually depletes them remains an open question. No clear depletion was found in mature software [24], whereas a decline was observed in OpenBSD after years of audits [25], and vulnerabilities in open-source code can survive for years before they are fixed [26]. These studies have described a lifecycle driven by humans and fuzzers. Since 2024, LLM-based systems have also been discovering and reporting vulnerabilities in real software. We therefore examine whether this lifecycle has changed, and measure on public records the time from the report to the fix and from disclosure to the first exploit and attack (Section VI).

Levels of autonomy. The SAE levels of driving automation define each level by the part of the task that remains with the human driver [16]. Similar levels have been proposed for general-purpose models and agents [27, 28]. These levels describe how a system is designed or deployed, so the same model can be placed at several levels. We adopt the structure of these scales, but we define each level by what a system has been shown to do on real targets, separately for each task. Frontier labs have also defined their own cyber capability thresholds, which determine the safeguards that a model requires before release [29, 30, 31]. These thresholds are assessed mostly through evaluations within each lab. Our map complements them with a comparison across labs, tiers and time that is based on real-world evidence.

Surveys and measurement. Existing surveys of LLMs in software security have organized the techniques and benchmarks for vulnerability detection [32, 33, 34, 35], repair [36, 37, 38, 39] and penetration testing [40, 41], and have reviewed security agents [42]. These surveys each focus on one part of vulnerability research, and they largely report results on benchmarks. Benchmarks evaluate models on capture-the-flag tasks and on reproduced or injected vulnerabilities [43, 14, 44, 45], so their scores do not establish what a system has achieved on real software or how much of the work remained with a human. Three lines of work are closer to ours. Security agents have been rated at each stage of vulnerability research by the depth of their results [46], recent work has argued that the bottleneck has moved from discovery to remediation [47], and government evaluators have used task suites to track frontier models and the pace at which open-weight models follow [48, 15, 49, 50].

To our knowledge, no prior work has assessed all four tasks on real software by both autonomy and correctness, dated each result, graded the evidence behind it and recorded who can access the system (Table I). The absence of such an assessment has made it difficult to compare the reports of labs, vendors and maintainers with one another, and to judge the expectations that are drawn from them. Our map provides this assessment. We further compare it with public vulnerability records and grade the proposed mitigations, which connects the demonstrated capability to its observed consequences and to the evidence for each response.

III Assessment Framework

Capabilities. We assess the four tasks of vulnerability research whose individual results can be checked (Table II). Choosing targets is captured by the highest level of the autonomy scale, and we return to deployment and disclosure, which have no comparable check, in Section VI. Three of the four capabilities can serve attackers and defenders alike, whereas patching is primarily defensive. Discovery and remediation each consist of a step that produces a result and a step that checks it. Discover means reporting weaknesses in a codebase, binary, or running service that prove to be real vulnerabilities, without being pointed to a candidate. Validate vulnerability means confirming or rejecting a candidate from any source and, when the candidate is real, producing a proof of vulnerability (PoV) such as a working exploit. A PoV is an input or procedure that shows that the flaw is real. Patch means delivering a fix that removes the cause without breaking the software, where passing the PoV and the tests is necessary but not sufficient [52, 53]. Validate patch means accepting correct fixes and rejecting wrong ones.

Scope. We assess vulnerability research on software, including source code, binaries, firmware, smart contracts and running web services. Our assessment ends at the proof that a vulnerability is real. This proof counts as validation even when it is a working exploit, and we report it only as an outcome. What an attacker does with the vulnerability afterwards, such as intrusion into a system, is outside our scope, as are social engineering and network configuration, which have no comparable check of correctness. Results on targets built or seeded for an evaluation, such as the vulnerabilities that the organizers of AIxCC injected into open-source projects, count as benchmark evidence.

Autonomy. The autonomy scale has six levels, from A0 to A5 (Table III). Following the SAE levels of driving automation [16], each level is defined by the work that remains with the human. At A0, the system contributes nothing to the task. At A1, it advises a human who performs every action, and at A2 it carries out the very specific steps that a human specifies. From A3 upward, the system plans and runs the task itself, and we refer to it as an LLM-based agent. At A3, a human still prepares each target or steps in when the agent gets stuck, whereas at A4 the agent completes the task on a given target without any human intervention. A human who checks the results afterwards does not lower the level, since this check is how correctness is measured. At A5, the agent also chooses its own targets and works across many of them over long periods.

Correctness. Correctness measures the capability of a system as the share of the outcomes it delivers, whether vulnerabilities, verdicts or patches, that are deemed correct by the party receiving them, such as the maintainer, the vendor or an independent reviewer (Table III). This share corresponds to the precision of the system. We chose it because every delivered result can be checked, whereas the vulnerabilities that a system misses in real software are unknown. It can also serve as a good proxy for the amount of human review that the results still require. Sources also report task completion, the share of the given targets for which a system delivers a result, and recall. We record both with each result and keep them separate from the category. Results are below the bar (C0) when most of them do not hold up, capable (C1) when most of them hold up, and expert (C2) when they hold up as often as an expert’s. We anchor expert to the expert rate published for the capability, or to about nine results in ten when none is published. Expert in audited code (C3) denotes expert precision on code that experts and fuzzers had examined for years. A system reaches an autonomy level only from C1 upward, so a level shown at C0 does not count. Where no source publishes a rate for a level that a system has demonstrated, the reviewing authors assign the category from the converging evidence on that result, such as fixes merged by maintainers, independent confirmation and the results of the same system on benchmarks.

Access and evidence. We assign each result an access tier, based on how widely the system behind it was available at the time of the evidence. T1 covers systems available only inside the organization that built them, T2 systems available to selected partners or sold through sales contacts, T3 systems that anyone can sign up for and T4 open-weight models. The tier corresponds to the access needed to use the system as it was evaluated, including both scaffold and model, so a proprietary scaffold on a public model counts at the tier of the scaffold. The tiers are cumulative, and a level counts for a tier once a system available at that tier or more widely has reached it. We also assign each result an evidence grade. E1 covers results reported by the organization that built the system, E2 results reported with checkable details such as named targets, advisories or logs, and E3 results confirmed by an independent party. Benchmarks, capture-the-flag challenges and competitions rely on targets built for the evaluation, we treat their results as complementary evidence. More anecdotal result, such as a small sample or a figure found only in secondary press, must be supported by additional evidence or benchmark scores before it can set a level. In contrast, a report that states its denominator over hundreds of results can set a level on its own. Several results that agree can set a level together, and a result on an adjacent task, such as porting an existing fix to an older release, can serve as corroboration.

Steps of the map. We describe each result as a pair of an autonomy level and a correctness category, for example A4 at expert (A4⋅\cdotC2), dated from the first source that shows both values for the same system. Each combination of a capability and an access tier is a cell of the map, and each dated pair in a cell is a step.

Bases. A value is direct when a source documents it on real-world software at that tier or more widely. The principal map and the answers to the research questions rest mainly on direct values, and the figures mark the other values. We report two other kinds of values separately. A benchmark value, marked ‡, comes from a realistic benchmark built from real vulnerabilities, such as PatchEval or CyberGym. It measures task completion on prepared targets and serves only as complementary evidence. An inferred value, marked †, is a hypothesis that a level shown directly on real-world software transfers to a more widely available model. We state such a hypothesis only when three conditions hold. The model must score at or above the model of the direct evidence on several independent measures, a scaffold that reaches the level must be available for it at the tier, and independent sources must corroborate the match. For a system with a direct level but no published rate, the hypothesis takes the measured accuracy of its model in the same role. Section V-C reports how the map changes with and without both kinds.

IV Methodology

Figure 2 summarizes how we collect and score the evidence.

IV-A Evidence Base

Search, indexing and screening. We began with a systematic search organized along the stages of the PRISMA guideline [54], from identification to screening and inclusion (Figure 7, Appendix A). We ran 67 queries on Semantic Scholar and arXiv and collected the reports of 105 organizations. Two LLM screeners independently judged the 13,982 records against written inclusion criteria and agreed on 94% of them (Cohen’s κ=0.87\kappa=0.87 [55]). After following the references and citations of the included works and adding the sources found by coding agents in three harnesses (Claude Code,11 1 https://claude.com/product/claude-code Codex22 2 https://openai.com/codex and Muse Code33 3 https://dev.meta.ai/products/muse-code), the search yielded 6,871 sources. Because many results on frontier systems are published only in blog posts, reports and news, we added two further sources of records. A search agent with 18 connectors returned 49,949 works from scholarly indexes, news sites, security mailing lists and forums such as Hacker News. We also collected lab reports, evaluations, vendor posts, maintainers’ accounts and incident reports. After merging duplicates, the corpus contains 53,057 sources. We indexed it for search by keyword, by dense embeddings of each source and of its passages, and through its citation graph, and a learned ranker combines these results. On held-out queries, the top ten results contained 92% of the relevant sources (Appendix A). The scoring and review agents used this search to retrieve the evidence for each cell. Two independent agents reviewed all the evidence and marked 9,859 of them as relevant, meaning that they report a result of an LLM-based system on a vulnerability research task.

Reading. Of the 9,859 relevant sources, 6,604 date from 2024 onwards and concern real-world software. A local LLM (Muse Glimmer 30B) read these sources and ranked them, and agents then read in full the 1,100 most likely to affect the results. For each source, they recorded the system, its autonomy level, access tier, evidence grade, date and correctness rate, and quoted a sentence from the source in support of each value. A script then confirmed that 99.6% of these quotes appear word for word in the sources. This check excludes invented quotes, and whether a quote supports its level is judged in the later stages and in the authors’ review. The scoring agents could also search the indexed corpus, and the runs that searched both the corpus and the web found no relevant source missing from it.

IV-B Scoring

The scoring gives, for each cell, the dates when each autonomy level was first reached, with the correctness reached at that level.

Scoring runs. Each scoring run scored one cell and returned its steps, each with the readings that support it. Every value had to quote its source, and a script checked the quote. Each cell was scored twice. One run started from the readings of systems available at that tier, whereas the other started without readings and searched the corpus and the web, in order to check whether the readings had missed evidence. Readers and scoring runs used Claude Sonnet 5.5, and all later agents used Claude Opus 5.5.

Decision. For each capability, a review agent compared the two runs of each cell, and a decision agent then decided the steps of each cell and justified each decision. The two runs agreed on whether a level had been reached in 83% of the comparisons. For each capability, one agent then argued for higher levels and another for lower levels, each unaware of the other. A verifier, which received their proposals anonymized and in random order, accepted 34 and rejected 30, and the remaining proposals were settled in the authors’ review.

Coverage round. To extend coverage, the local LLM read 20,631 further sources, and Claude agents checked each candidate against the source text. This round added 55 steps and revised 18 others, most often by lowering a level that were over-estimated.

Authors’ review. Two of the authors manually and independently validated the map in two stages. In the first, they scored the 16 most recent cells themselves and agreed with the pipeline on the autonomy level of 10 of them (63%). This comparison led them to state their scoring preferences, including the corroboration rule of Section III, and the pipeline then rescored the whole map under these rules. In the second stage, they reviewed every step of the resulting map against its sources. They agreed with the pipeline on the highest level of 15 of the 16 cells (94%) and on the level of 107 of the 119 steps that they kept (90%). Where the pipeline had also assigned a correctness category, they confirmed the full pair for 82 of 94 steps (87%), and the other 12 pairs differed by at most one level and one category. For 25 steps without a published rate, they assigned the category from the converging evidence, and they added four steps. The final map contains 128 steps. Of these, 85 rest on direct evidence and form the principal map, while 35 are benchmark values and 8 are inferred values, which we report separately. The two authors agreed with each other on the autonomy level of 88% of the steps that both rated (Cohen’s κ=0.83\kappa=0.83), a rate similar to their agreement with the pipeline. Appendix C lists every step with its sources.

IV-C Records and Statements

To answer RQ4 and RQ5, we combined statements with public records. Separate agents with web access collected statements on consequences and defenses from frontier labs and vendors, practitioners, maintainers, government agencies and the academic literature. We kept the 503 statements whose quote could be verified on its source page, and derived from them the questions that we examine and the defenses that we grade.

We measure five quantities from public records (Appendix B). The volume and severity of disclosures come from the CVE List of 31 October 2026 [17], which holds 304,028 records published since 2018 with their issuer, weakness type, severity scores and finder credits. The involvement of LLM-based systems comes from about 2,600 of these records, which name such a system as finder in the credits of advisories or in the lists published by labs and vendors. The age of the vulnerable code comes from the release that introduced each vulnerability, which can be dated for the Linux kernel, Windows, open-source packages and other software with dated releases. The time from report to fix comes from the advisories of the Zero Day Initiative since 2016 [56] and from Chrome’s public bug tracker [57]. The time to exploitation comes from the first public exploit code in Exploit-DB, Metasploit and proof-of-concept repositories on GitHub [58, 59, 60], and from the listing as exploited in CISA’s catalogue [61]. We complement these records with the public reports of disclosure programs, namely the dashboards of Anthropic and Patch the Planet [62, 63], the trackers of Project Zero and Big Sleep [64, 65] and the statistics of syzbot [66].

V Demonstrated Capability

Figure 1 shows the highest pair reached in each cell by 7 November 2026, and Figure 3 its evolution since 2024. The results below rest on direct evidence on real-world software, for the systems and targets that the sources report, and we mark the values that come from a benchmark (‡) or from inference (†). Appendix C lists the evidence behind every step.

V-A RQ1: Autonomy Today

Discovery and validation. LLM-based agents have been shown to discover and validate vulnerabilities without human intervention at expert correctness (A4⋅\cdotC2) at every tier. At the partner tier, Claude Mythos Preview extended this correctness in May 2026 to code that experts and fuzzers had examined for years (A4⋅\cdotC3), and independent firms confirmed 90.6% of its 1,752 assessed findings [4, 12]. Public systems reached expert correctness (A4⋅\cdotC2) around the same time, when a security firm confirmed 96% of the findings of Aikido Attack, a commercial agent that anyone can sign up for [67]. Open-weight models followed within months. GLM 5.3, released in August 2026 and assessed by the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation as the most capable open-weight model to date [49], developed end-to-end exploits at a rate close to that of Mythos Preview on a benchmark of browser-engine vulnerabilities (‡) [68]. In addition, on real software, 94.5% of the reports that a published harness produced with DeepSeek V4 Pro on a production codebase proved true in October 2026 [69].

At the lab tier, agents have also become capable of choosing their own targets and completing attacks end-to-end (A5⋅\cdotC1). In July 2026, agents under evaluation at OpenAI turned to third-party systems without human direction and, over days to weeks, found and exploited previously unknown vulnerabilities in them [6], which Hugging Face and METR independently confirmed [70, 71]. Similar events have since been reported for models from labs including Anthropic and Meta, in the labs’ own use and in external evaluations [72, 73, 74].

Patching. Agents have also been shown to patch without human intervention, at capable correctness on public models (A4⋅\cdotC1) and at expert correctness at the partner tier (A4⋅\cdotC2). By October 2025, Google’s CodeMender had upstreamed 72 security fixes to open-source projects [75], and maintainers had merged the fixes written by a depthfirst agent for Netty and by the open-source PortGPT agent for the Linux kernel [76, 77]. Expert correctness was reached around September 2026 by initiatives like OpenAI’s Defense Factory, a production pipeline for partners in which 0.53% of the fixes were rolled back [78]. For open-weight models, we infer A4 at capable correctness (A4⋅\cdotC1†). On a benchmark of real CVEs, DeepSeek V4 Flash fixed about as many vulnerabilities as GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, 80% against 81 to 84% [79], and the open-source PortGPT agent, whose kernel fixes maintainers merged, also runs on open-weight models [77].

Patch validation. Agents have been checking their own patches without human intervention (A4⋅\cdotC1) since October 2025. Google’s CodeMender and AISLE’s remediation system each described an agent that tested its patches for the root cause and for regressions, and passed on only those that held [75, 80]. Public systems followed in April 2026 [81, 82]. At the partner tier, patch validation reached expert correctness (A4⋅\cdotC2) in the Defense Factory, where the fixes that the pipeline let through were rarely rolled back [78]. On a benchmark of real CVE fixes (‡), an LLM judge agreed with a careful human reading in 85% of the cases [83]. Open-weight models have reached A3⋅\cdotC1 on real software [84], and a reviewer agent on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash reached A4⋅\cdotC1 on a benchmark (‡) in October 2026 [85].

Across tiers. Of the 16 cells, 14 have reached A4 or A5 on direct evidence, and open-weight patching reaches A4 by inference (Figure 1). Open-weight patch validation stands at A3⋅\cdotC1 on real software, and reaches A4 on a benchmark. The highest steps of discovery and validation at the lab, partner and public tiers are independently confirmed (E3), those of patching rest on checkable reports (E2), and those of patch validation mostly on the developers’ own reports (E1), which makes remediation the least measured part of the map.

V-B RQ2: Change Since 2024

Since 2024, the highest autonomy level of every task has risen steadily, one level at a time (Figure 3). Each level has first been reached at capable correctness and later at expert correctness. In 2024, LLMs mostly performed individual steps inside pipelines designed by humans (A2⋅\cdotC1), such as writing fuzz targets or drafting a fix for a scanner alert [87]. The first agents able to plan the whole task (A3⋅\cdotC1) appeared in the same year and were able to find zero-days that received CVE identifiers [88, 1]. These agents reached expert correctness (A3⋅\cdotC2) in May 2025, when maintainers confirmed or fixed 94% of the bugs reported by RepoAudit [89].

Discovery and validation reached A4 in mid-2025. The XBOW agent reached capable correctness (A4⋅\cdotC1) around June, when the programs on HackerOne judged 72% of its 886 closed reports to be genuine [90]. Expert correctness (A4⋅\cdotC2) followed in August, when an agentic system for Android apps confirmed 97% of its reported zero-days [91]. In May 2026, Mythos Preview extended expert correctness to code audited for years (A4⋅\cdotC3), where it was able to find thousands of validated vulnerabilities [4, 12].

Patching and patch validation reached A4 at capable correctness (C1) in October 2025, four months after discovery. Expert correctness (C2) followed in September 2026, in initiatives like OpenAI’s Defense Factory [78]. This later date is likely to reflect how rarely the correctness of patches is reported in the literature, since patches written at lower autonomy (A2) had already reached expert correctness (C2) by mid-2025 (Appendix C).

Open-weight models followed in the same order. For discovery and validation, they reached A4 at capable correctness (C1) in April 2026, when Chrome confirmed the vulnerabilities reported by an agent on Kimi K2.5 [92]. Expert correctness (A4⋅\cdotC2) followed for both tasks in October 2026 [69], and we infer A4⋅\cdotC1 for patching from August 2026 (†).

V-C RQ3: Spread to Public and Open Weights

Public and open-weight systems have reached each level within months of the first system to show it (Table IV). At capable correctness (A4⋅\cdotC1), public systems followed within 7 months for every task, and open-weight models after about 10 months for discovery and validation. At expert correctness (A4⋅\cdotC2), public systems followed after about 9 months for discovery and validation, and open-weight models after about a year. For patching and patch validation, the inferred and benchmark values place open-weight models 10 to 12 months behind the first system (†).

These delays are upper bounds, since they date the first documented use on real software, and the models themselves appear to spread faster. The open-weight GLM 5.3 was released four months after Mythos Preview became available to partners [106]. In Anthropic’s comparison, it developed end-to-end exploits about as often as Mythos Preview, in 12% of 410 attempts against 14% [68], and the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation placed it about four months behind the US frontier [49]. On twelve security benchmarks, open-weight models tend to reach the scores of closed models about 8 months later (5.4 to 10.0, Figure 4), which is consistent with the 4 to 7 months reported by the UK AI Security Institute and Epoch AI [15, 50].

Ablations. Table IX (Appendix C) presents the map under four evidence standards. Apart from open-weight patching, which is marked as inferred, none of the answers above depends on a benchmark or inferred value of the map. When only results with checkable details or independent confirmation (E2 or E3) are kept, discovery and validation reach A4 in August 2025 instead of June, patch validation reaches A4 only in September 2026 at the lab and partner tiers, and it falls to A3 at the public tier, so that 13 of the 16 cells reach A4 or A5.

VI Observed Consequences

To answer RQ4, we compare the consequences commonly expected of LLM-based vulnerability research with public records since 2024. We derived seven such consequences from the 503 verified statements, on which labs, maintainers, agencies and researchers may have diverging analyses, and Table V sets their positions against what has been demonstrated and what the public records show. From the records, we measure the number of disclosures, their severity, the age of the vulnerable code, the finders who report them, and the time from report to fix and from disclosure to attack (Figure 6). Since few records name the tool behind a finding, these measures date the changes, and the share of each that is due to LLM-based systems remains to be determined. Where we compare the records that name an AI system as finder with other records, we use the other records of the same issuers as the comparison group.

Disclosures more than doubled. The number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled in 2026. CVE records [17] published from January to October rose from 39,638 in 2025 to 89,749 in 2026, and the monthly count nearly quadrupled, from 4,302 in January 2026 to 16,949 in October (Figures 5 and 6a). The increase extended to every class of vulnerability and to about two thirds of the largest organizations that issue CVE records. Two thirds of it came from six of these issuers, namely GitHub, VulnCheck, Oracle, the Linux kernel, Chrome and Microsoft [17]. The records that vendors and projects issue for their own software rose 2.8 times, after growing by at most 1.3 times a year from 2019 to 2025. Those of third-party issuers, such as researchers and bug bounty programs, rose 1.6 times, although they had grown faster than those of vendors since 2022 (Appendix B). Records that name an AI system as finder rose from 268 in 2025 to 2,290 in the first ten months of 2026, or 2.4 to 2.8% of all records in each quarter. Since most records name no tool, this count is a lower bound [96]. Since vendors had access to their code throughout, this reversal suggests that the owners of code have gained the most from LLM-based discovery so far.

A growing share of disclosed vulnerabilities is rated Critical or High. The share of these records rated Critical or High rose from 46% in 2025 to 56% from July to October 2026 [17] (Figure 6b). The rise holds when the comparison is limited to the same issuers and to the same types of vulnerability. With the set of issuers fixed to that of 2025, the share has risen every year since 2023, and fastest in 2026 (Appendix B). Throughout 2026, the records that name an AI system as finder had about the same share as the other records of their issuers. This trend is consistent with LLM-based systems and other new tools uncovering severe vulnerabilities that had remained hidden.

Old, severe bugs surface more often. Severe bugs that had survived a decade or more were reported several times more often in 2026. Where the age of the vulnerable code is known, bugs at least ten years old and rated Critical or High were reported 6 to 11 times as often per month from July to October 2026 as in 2025, in the Linux kernel, Windows, open-source packages and other software with dated releases [17, 100] (Figure 6c). Most of this increase followed the overall rise in records, and the share of old bugs among dated records rose by 6 to 9 points. The age is known for most kernel records but for only 2 to 3% of the others, so this measure covers a part of all software (Appendix B). This rise is consistent with the capability shown in RQ1, where agents found vulnerabilities in code that experts and fuzzers had examined for years (A4⋅\cdotC3). Forecasts that the surge will end once existing code has been swept assume that vulnerabilities are sparse [10, 11], in Schneier’s term, rather than plentiful [117, 118]. In the code that we could date, the records show no sign of exhaustion so far.

Most credits go to first-time finders. The CVE records that name a finder, 43% of those of 2026, credited 2.6 times as many distinct finders from January to October as a year earlier, for 2.1 times as many records [17]. Finders who had never been credited before received 70% of these credits, whereas this share had fallen every year from 2022 to 2025, to 51%. This suggests that vulnerability discovery has become accessible to finders without an established record, as public and open-weight systems become increasingly capable (RQ3).

The time to fix has not shifted. The time from report to fix has not shifted noticeably. The Zero Day Initiative gives vendors 120 days to fix a vulnerability [119], and publishes the dates of each report and release. In a sample of 1,417 of its advisories, the median time from report to release of fixed cases stayed between 96 and 119 days in every year from 2016 to 2026 (Figure 6d). The most recent quarter, which covers six weeks and 28 fixed cases, has the highest median of the series, at 148 days, above this deadline. Chrome fixed external reports in a median of 50 days from 2020 to 2023, 44 in 2025 and 36 to 45 in 2026, and reports that name an AI system as finder in 16 to 26 days. So far, vendors have therefore kept meeting the deadline of coordinated disclosure, and Chrome has fixed the reports that name an AI system faster than the others. Whether a report is fixed at all appears to depend on how it reaches the owner of the code (Table VI). Three vendors shipped fixes for their own code at many times their earlier rate. In contrast, only 5 to 26% of the reports sent in bulk to outside maintainers were fixed, a share that predates LLMs, whereas curated programs and OSS-Fuzz reached 58 to 94%. Most reports sent in bulk thus remain unfixed, which is where a larger number of findings is most likely to exceed the capacity to fix. Since these programs differ in targets, validity, severity and age, the differences cannot be attributed to the way a report is sent alone.

The time to attack has not shortened. The time from disclosure to attack has not shortened noticeably either. CISA lists a CVE in its catalogue of known exploited vulnerabilities once it has reliable evidence of an attack. For CVEs listed within 90 days of their record, the median time from record to listing was 2 to 5 days in every year from 2022 to 2026, the last covering records published up to mid-July, and 24 to 30% of the entries of each year were listed on or before the day of the record, with no trend (Figure 6d). Mandiant’s mean time from patch to first observed attack fell from 63 days in 2018 and 2019 to 5 days in 2023, before LLM-based systems were finding vulnerabilities in real software, and to an estimated −7-7 days in 2025 [103]. Public exploit code did not appear earlier either, with a median of 5 days after the record in 2026 against 1 to 2 days from 2020 to 2025. Observed attacks have thus not yet followed what demonstrations show to be possible. Starting from public patches, Mythos Preview was able to write browser-engine exploits within hours [9], and the open-weight GLM 5.3 developed attacks against six Firefox releases using only the information that was public at each release [105]. Incidents confirm that attackers have used LLM-based agents [146, 147, 148], but no source yet attributes a measurable share of intrusions to them [103].

Our reading. Defenders may have absorbed a larger number of more severe findings at an unchanged pace, or attackers may not yet use these systems at scale or in ways that the catalogues capture, and the records cannot yet distinguish between the two.

VII Mitigations and Guidance

To answer RQ5, Table VII lists the mitigations proposed in response to LLM-based vulnerability research, grouped by their goal, and grades the evidence that it works. The grade combines the four attributes of the best evidence defined in the caption. Evidence is strong for a security outcome in deployment that is confirmed and not reported by a vendor alone, moderate for any measured outcome on real software that is not reported by a vendor alone, and weak otherwise. The grades describe how well a mitigation works in general, since no source tests one against LLM-based attackers.

What follows from our findings. The best-supported mitigations are established practices of secure design and maintenance, such as memory-safe languages, a smaller attack surface, compartmentalization and automatic updates. Most mitigations built on LLMs have so far been measured only in vendor reports and benchmarks. Our findings suggest three points (D). First, finding vulnerabilities may no longer be what limits defenders. Agents have been shown to find them at expert correctness at every tier, yet in the programs we measured most reports sent in bulk to outside maintainers remain unfixed, whereas three vendors report shipping many times more fixes after scanning their own code (Section VI). LLM-based discovery thus seems to help most where the fix is made. Second, the critical delay may now be the time to deploy a fix, since exploits have been built from public fixes within hours in demonstrations, while Verizon reports that organizations had fully remediated only 26% of known exploited vulnerabilities in 2025 [149]. Third, restricting frontier models delays the spread of these capabilities by months only (RQ3), and defenses should assume that attackers have them. Defenders therefore seem to need LLM-based systems that find, fix and detect at the pace of attacks, built on a secure design that limits what any missed vulnerability allows.

Guidance by stakeholder. Items marked D are our deductions, which the records have not tested.

  • •

    Maintainers and vendors should run LLM-based discovery on their own code, write new code in memory-safe languages and remove code that need not be reachable. Those with early access to restricted models should sweep their most exposed code first (D).

  • •

    Operators should apply updates by default, merge automatic dependency updates after tests, and measure their time to deploy (D). Until a fix is deployed, compartmentalization limits what an attacker gains. Least privilege with phishing-resistant authentication, isolating systems that get no updates and automated detection and response are also advised, with no measured effect yet.

  • •

    Finders who use LLM-based systems should send maintainers only reports they have confirmed, each with a proposed fix, and publish how many targets and reports each result comes from (D).

  • •

    Coordinators, bounty programs and funders should pay for review, patches and backports more than for further findings, and have records name the tool that found a vulnerability (D).

  • •

    Evaluators and policymakers should test released models on real software, plan for open-weight parity within months and track our indicators (D).

VIII Open Problems

Removing vulnerability classes from existing code. The strong evidence for memory-safe languages concerns new code, whereas decade-old severe bugs now surface several times more often. LLMs have translated programs and libraries of a few thousand lines at most from C to safe Rust [150, 151] and produced no-crash proofs for fuzzing entry points of over a hundred libraries, for bounded inputs [129]. Yet a benchmark finds them weak at writing code, specification and proof together [152], and verified systems have failed mostly at their unverified interfaces [153]. Scaling both to large code bases is open.

Secure architecture by construction. Retrofitting compartmentalization and least privilege requires engineering for each component [154, 155], and zero trust rests on advice so far. We found no evaluation of agents that derive and enforce such boundaries beyond single components.

Remediation at the pace of discovery. Most bulk reports remain unfixed, and patch validation is the least measured task. Validators with known error rates, compared on benchmarks of known vulnerabilities [45], are open, as is deploying fixes before their code is public, since exploits can be built from it [9, 105].

Disclosure when findings collide. Linux maintainers now ask that a bug found with an LLM be treated as public [156], and in October 2026 three parties reported the same PHP flaw within six weeks, with exploitation attempts before the embargo ended [157, 158]. Coordinating such collisions is open.

Defenses tested against LLM-based attackers. No source behind Table VII tests a mitigation against an LLM-based attacker, and few records name the tool behind a finding or an intrusion. Such tests and records would show whether attacks follow the demonstrations.

Contained agents. Agents under evaluation have left their environment [6, 72], and detection agents read data that attackers control [142, 143]. Containing a system that can find vulnerabilities in its own sandbox is open.

IX Conclusion

We separated what LLM-based systems have been shown to do in vulnerability research from what has changed in public records. On direct evidence, agents were able to discover, validate and patch real vulnerabilities without human intervention (A4) by October 2025, and restricted capabilities reached open-weight models within months. Discovery and validation have since reached expert correctness at every tier (A4⋅\cdotC2). In 2026, the number of CVE records more than doubled, a growing share was rated Critical or High, and severe bugs present for a decade or more surfaced several times more often. Yet the time from report to fix and from disclosure to listed attack has not shifted noticeably so far. Whether this pace holds as findings grow, and whether attacks follow the demonstrations, remains to be measured.

Appendix A Corpus and Search

Search. The corpus is indexed by keyword (BM25 [159]), by dense embeddings of each source and of its passages (Qwen3-Embedding-4B [160]), and through its citation graph. A learned ranker (LambdaMART [161]) combines these results with a cross-encoder reranker [160]. We evaluated it on 256 queries, with relevance pooled as in TREC [162] from the top 20 results of every search mode and graded by the local LLM (weighted κ≈0.70\kappa\approx 0.70 with Claude on 600 pairs). We tuned on 177 queries and report the other 79 in Table VIII.

Appendix B Measurement Details

Records. The counts of records in Section VI use the public CVE List as of 31 October 2026. A record names an AI system as finder when its credit, or a list published by a lab or vendor, names an LLM-based system or its operator. A record is rated Critical or High when its CVSS base score is 7 or more, and we take the issuer’s score, else CISA’s, else NVD’s. With the issuers of 2025 held fixed, the share rated Critical or High was 38% in 2023, 42% in 2024, 46% in 2025 and 57% from July to October 2026. An issuer is third-party when the CVE Program lists it with none of the types Vendor, Open Source, Hosted Service or Consortium [164], or when it covers WordPress plugins.

Age, finders and time. The age of a bug is the time from the release that introduced it to its fix. A finder is an identity named in the credit of a record, and it is first-time when no earlier record since 2018 credits it. The time to fix comes from a sample of 1,417 of the 14,738 advisories of the Zero Day Initiative, stratified by quarter of release [119], in which no credit names an AI system. The time to attack and to public exploit code covers the records with at least 104 days of follow-up.

Figures. In Figure 5, the records that credit an LLM-based system grew 8.8 times a year from July 2025 to September 2026 (95% interval 5.3 to 14.8). The scenario slows this growth to a peak in the window when three practitioners expect the surge to end, and then lets it decline with a half-life of 10 to 24 months. The cost projections continue the measured curves and ease within a few months to a decline of 4.7 times a year, the rate that Epoch AI reports for a level of performance two years after its debut [114]. In Figure 4, we fit 104 best scores with one slope, one offset per benchmark and one shift for open-weight models, which gives a delay of 7.6 months (95% bootstrap interval 5.4 to 10.0).

Appendix C The Final Map

Table C lists the 128 steps of the final map with their sources, and Table IX the highest pair of each cell under four evidence standards. Tiers are cumulative, so a step of a more widely available system counts at every more restricted tier. A result can set a higher pair at a tier where further sources corroborate it than at a tier where it stands alone, as for the firmware agent of November 2025 at the public and open-weight tiers. A step carries an earlier date at a more restricted tier when its system was available there first, such as a tool that its authors used before releasing it. A question mark marks a level without a correctness category, † an inferred value and ‡ a benchmark value, and the principal map uses the 85 direct steps, which carry neither mark. The reports of the June 2025 step were reviewed by the vendor’s staff before submission, and without this step A4 dates from August 2025. Direct evidence has confirmed or preceded seven of the eight inferred values, and the eighth, open-weight patching at A4⋅\cdotC1, remains untested on real software. The full table of readings, with the rate behind each correctness category, is released with our artifact.
